title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Five distinct financial engines—from 60%-margin card toll-booths to $4.4-trillion money-center banks—share one roof inside XLF, and each responds differently to the macro cycle.
epigraph.author: XLF Look-Through Business Disaggregation

web_blocks.text: 2.1 Five GICS Industry Groups and Top-10 Concentration Inside XLF
web_blocks.title: 2.1 Five GICS Industry Groups and Top-10 Concentration Inside XLF

web_blocks.html: Unlike a single firm, XLF is a modified market-cap-weighted basket of 76 S&P 500 financial stocks. These firms span five GICS industry groups. As of November 23, 2026 (SSGA official data), those five groups are Financial Services (32.30%), Banks (25.52%), Capital Markets (24.27%), Insurance (14.15%), and Consumer Finance (3.76%). Top-end weight is high: the top 10 holdings make up 57.17% of fund assets. The top four alone—Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard—account for 39.83%. To judge XLF well, we must study how each of these five engines makes money rather than treating financials as a plain bank proxy.

web_blocks.text: 2.2 Segment 1: Financial Services & Payment Networks (32.30% of XLF)
web_blocks.title: 2.2 Segment 1: Financial Services & Payment Networks (32.30% of XLF)

web_blocks.html: Financial Services is XLF's largest and highest-quality group. It pairs Berkshire Hathaway (13.61%) with global payment rails led by Visa (8.91%), Mastercard (6.56%), Fiserv, PayPal, and Block/Global Payments. Unlike banks, payment networks run asset-light digital rails with high margins. They ride global spending growth and inflation without taking borrower default risk onto their own books. In FY2026 (ended September 30, 2026), Visa posted $45.9 billion in net revenue (+15% YoY) and $23.5 billion in GAAP net income (+17% YoY). Its Value-Added Services (fraud checks, tokenization, cyber-risk) jumped 30% to $14 billion. Mastercard posted ~$32.8 billion in FY2025 net revenue and $18.90 billion in operating profit, with Value-Added Services reaching 40.6% of total sales.

Concrete End-to-End Real-World Example (Visa / Mastercard Four-Party Card Swipe): Picture a small-business traveler in Chicago paying a $200 hotel bill with a Chase Visa card. The guest wants fast, safe checkout without cash; the hotel wants sure settlement within 24 hours. When the card taps the reader, the merchant's acquirer sends the request over VisaNet to JPMorgan Chase in milliseconds. The hotel pays a ~$4.00–$4.40 (~2.0%–2.2%) merchant discount fee. Chase keeps most of that fee (~1.7%–1.8% interchange) to fund card rewards and cover credit risk. The merchant acquirer takes a ~0.2% processing slice. Visa collects roughly $0.25–$0.35 (12–18 bps) in network, data, and token fees, with zero loan risk and >60% operating margins. In the same segment, Berkshire Hathaway takes upfront premiums at GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance. Its $176 billion in insurance float (FY2025) produced $7.26 billion in underwriting profit and $12.51 billion in insurance investment income, held mostly in short-term U.S. Treasury Bills.

web_blocks.text: 2.3 Segment 2: Diversified & Money-Center Banks (25.52% of XLF)
web_blocks.title: 2.3 Segment 2: Diversified & Money-Center Banks (25.52% of XLF)

web_blocks.html: America's Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) anchor XLF's Banks group. The leaders are JPMorgan Chase (10.75%), Bank of America (4.00%), Wells Fargo (3.09%), and Citigroup (2.45%). Super-regionals like U.S. Bancorp, PNC Financial, and Truist sit right behind them. Banks make money in two ways: Net Interest Income (NII)—the spread between loan yields and deposit costs—and Non-Interest Fee Income from cash services, cards, wealth advice, and deal fees. In FY2025, JPMorgan Chase earned $57.0 billion in GAAP net income ($20.02 EPS) on $185 billion in managed revenue. It posted 20% ROTCE across $4.4 trillion in assets. Bank of America earned $30.5 billion in net income on $113.1 billion in revenue. Wells Fargo had its seven-year Federal Reserve asset cap lifted in 2025, lifting loan and deposit growth to ~11% YoY with a 16.3% ROTCE.

Concrete End-to-End Real-World Example (JPMorgan Chase Deposit-to-Middle-Market Loan Spread): Suppose a Midwest medical-device maker needs a $25 million working-capital credit line for hospital stock and payroll. Meanwhile, millions of U.S. households keep daily checking cash at Chase branches and on the Chase app. Those accounts pay just 0.01%–0.50% interest because users value direct deposit, Zelle, and wide ATM access. JPMorgan pools these sticky, low-cost deposits well below wholesale money-market rates. It then lends the $25 million line at SOFR + 225 bps (~6.5%–7.0%). At the same time, Chase cross-sells ACH payroll, currency hedges, and business cards. Even after CECL credit reserves and branch or tech costs, the spread (~3.39% industry NIM in Q3 2026) and treasury fees yield high-teens returns on tangible equity.

web_blocks.text: 2.4 Segment 3: Capital Markets, Asset Management & Market Infrastructure (24.27% of XLF)
web_blocks.title: 2.4 Segment 3: Capital Markets, Asset Management & Market Infrastructure (24.27% of XLF)

web_blocks.html: Capital Markets is XLF's third major pillar, blending three distinct models. First are investment banks and wealth firms like Goldman Sachs (3.06%), Morgan Stanley (2.63%), and Charles Schwab. Second are global asset managers led by BlackRock (2.11%), KKR, Blackstone, and Apollo. Third are toll-booth data, rating, and exchange leaders: S&P Global (SPGI), Moody's, CME Group, ICE, and MSCI. In FY2025, Morgan Stanley posted record net revenue of $70.6 billion and 21.6% ROTCE by pairing trading with sticky wealth fees. Goldman Sachs grew net revenue 9% to $58.3 billion with 15.0% ROE, climbing to 18.7% annualized in Q3 2026. Goldman also held its #1 global M&A spot for a 23rd straight year. Meanwhile, BlackRock reached $14.04 trillion in AUM ($24.22B revenue, +19% YoY). S&P Global lifted adjusted operating margins to 50.4%, with 65% margins in Ratings and 70% in Indices.

Concrete End-to-End Real-World Example (S&P Global Debt Issuance & BlackRock Aladdin/iShares): Suppose a Fortune 500 industrial firm sells $2 billion of 10-year senior bonds to buy a factory. Pension buyers require an outside credit grade before they touch the debt. The firm hires Goldman Sachs or Morgan Stanley to sell the bonds for ~0.6%–0.8% in deal fees. It also pays S&P Global Ratings a required rating fee (often 6–8 bps of deal size) plus yearly review fees. That toll yields a 65% segment operating margin with almost no capital tied up. Once issued, the bonds enter fixed-income indices run by BlackRock iShares ETFs. Buyers then track their risk daily on BlackRock's Aladdin platform, driving steady AUM fees and +16% organic software ACV growth in FY2025.

web_blocks.text: 2.5 Segment 4: Property & Casualty, Life & Specialty Insurance (14.15% of XLF)
web_blocks.title: 2.5 Segment 4: Property & Casualty, Life & Specialty Insurance (14.15% of XLF)

web_blocks.html: XLF's Insurance sleeve holds elite risk underwriters. Key names include Chubb (CB), Progressive (PGR), Marsh & McLennan, Aon, Travelers, Allstate, Aflac, and MetLife. Top P&C insurers earn money twice. First, they price risk cleanly to keep their Combined Ratio (claims plus costs divided by earned premiums) below 100%. Second, they invest upfront premium float in safe, investment-grade bonds. In FY2025, Chubb wrote $54.84 billion in net premiums ($53.0B earned) at a record-low 85.7% P&C combined ratio, yielding $6.53 billion in pure underwriting profit. Progressive earned $81.66 billion in net premiums (up from $58.67B in FY2023) at an 87.4% combined ratio. By October 2026, Progressive reached 28.22 million personal auto policies (+6.4% YoY) while earning $3.58 billion in investment income.

Concrete End-to-End Real-World Example (Progressive Telematics Auto Underwriting): A suburban commuter with a clean record faces rising auto-repair and medical costs. She wants fairer rates than old age-or-zip-code pricing offers, so she joins Progressive's Snapshot program. Snapshot tracks real-time braking, miles driven, and time of day. Progressive uses actuarial models to price her six-month policy upfront and takes $900 in cash on day one. Over the policy term, it pays out roughly $787 in claims, repair bills, and sales costs (an 87.4% combined ratio). That leaves ~$113 in pure underwriting profit, plus 4.5%–5.0% bond yields on the cash float while claims wait to settle.

web_blocks.text: 2.6 Segment 5: Consumer Finance & Closed-Loop Payments (3.76% of XLF)
web_blocks.title: 2.6 Segment 5: Consumer Finance & Closed-Loop Payments (3.76% of XLF)

web_blocks.html: Consumer Finance is XLF's smallest group at 3.76%, yet it holds high-ROE spend leaders. The core names are American Express (AXP), Capital One Financial (COF), and Synchrony Financial. Unlike Visa and Mastercard's open four-party setup, American Express runs a closed-loop network. Amex acts as card issuer, network, and merchant acquirer all at once. That lets it keep the full merchant fee and steep annual card fees while lending to high-FICO spenders. In FY2025, Amex handled $1,670 billion ($1.67 trillion) in global spend at an average 2.24% merchant fee and added 12.5 million new cards. By Q3 2026, Amex's card fee revenue hit $2.97 billion in one quarter (+16% YoY), or $136 per card per year.

Concrete End-to-End Real-World Example (American Express Platinum Closed-Loop Ecosystem): A corporate consultant pays $695+ a year for an Amex Platinum card. She gets Centurion airport lounges, travel credits, and high-tier points. When she puts a $1,000 flight and dinner on the card, Amex captures the full ~2.24% merchant fee ($22.40) directly. That slice is nearly 10x Visa's network fee. Amex also keeps her yearly card fee and any balance interest, while tight credit screens on affluent buyers keep loan losses low.

book_paragraphs: When you buy a single operating business, you usually have one core product engine to dissect. When you and I open the hood of XLF, we are actually looking at five completely different business models bolted onto one chassis. As of November 23, 2026, State Street's official holdings breakdown splits XLF into Financial Services at 32.30 percent, Banks at 25.52 percent, Capital Markets at 24.27 percent, Insurance at 14.15 percent, and Consumer Finance at 3.76 percent. Ten mega-cap titans make up 57.17 percent of the fund, and the top four alone—Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard—command nearly forty percent of your capital. Let us walk through each of those five engines with a real-world transaction so you can feel exactly how every dollar of profit is manufactured.

Start with XLF's largest and highest-quality pillar: Financial Services at 32.30 percent. This sleeve pairs Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway at 13.61 percent with the global payment toll-booths Visa at 8.91 percent and Mastercard at 6.56 percent. Picture a small-business traveler in Chicago tapping a Chase Visa card to pay a two-hundred-dollar hotel bill. The traveler wants frictionless, fraud-protected checkout; the hotel wants guaranteed cash tomorrow morning. In milliseconds, VisaNet routes that authorization between the merchant's bank and JPMorgan Chase. Out of roughly four dollars in merchant fees, Chase keeps the lion's share to fund rewards and cover default risk, while Visa clips around twenty-five to thirty-five cents purely for running the digital rails and fraud analytics. Visa never lends a dime to the traveler and takes zero credit-loss risk—which is why Visa generated $45.9 billion in net revenue and $23.5 billion in GAAP net income in fiscal 2026 with operating margins north of sixty percent. Sitting right next to Visa inside this same segment is Berkshire Hathaway, which holds $176 billion in insurance float that produced $7.26 billion in underwriting profit and $12.51 billion in investment income in 2025.

Second is traditional Banking at 25.52 percent, anchored by America's money-center fortresses: JPMorgan Chase at 10.75 percent, Bank of America at 4.00 percent, Wells Fargo at 3.09 percent, and Citigroup at 2.45 percent. Here, the economic engine is classic financial intermediation upgraded by massive digital scale. Imagine a Midwestern medical-device maker needing a twenty-five-million-dollar credit line to fund hospital inventory. On the other side of the ledger, millions of everyday households keep their checking accounts at Chase or Bank of America earning near-zero interest because their paychecks, mortgages, and Zelle transfers are anchored there. The bank gathers those sticky, low-cost deposits and lends them to the manufacturer at a healthy spread—roughly 3.39 percent across the FDIC-insured industry in the third quarter of 2026—while cross-selling payroll processing and foreign-exchange services. At JPMorgan's $4.4-trillion scale, that machine produced $57.0 billion in 2025 net income and a twenty percent return on tangible common equity. Meanwhile, Wells Fargo saw its seven-year Federal Reserve asset cap lifted in 2025, unleashing eleven percent loan and deposit growth and lifting its ROTCE to 16.3 percent.

Third is Capital Markets at 24.27 percent—an eclectic powerhouse blending Wall Street dealmakers like Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, asset-gathering giant BlackRock, and data-and-ratings oligopolies like S&P Global and Moody's. Picture a Fortune 500 manufacturer issuing two billion dollars of ten-year bonds to acquire a rival. Goldman Sachs or Morgan Stanley underwrites and places the debt, earning advisory and syndication fees—an engine that drove Goldman to $58.3 billion in 2025 revenue and Morgan Stanley to a record $70.6 billion and 21.6 percent ROTCE. Before pension funds will touch those bonds, however, the issuer must pay S&P Global Ratings a mandatory toll to stamp a credit grade on the paper, a franchise earning 65 percent operating margins. Once those bonds trade, they flow straight into BlackRock's $14.04 trillion asset-management ecosystem and get risk-tracked on its Aladdin software platform, earning recurring basis-point fees year after year.

Fourth is Insurance at 14.15 percent, led by disciplined property-and-casualty underwriters like Chubb and Progressive. Great insurers get paid twice. When a suburban driver signs up for Progressive's Snapshot telematics program, Progressive uses real-time driving data to price her six-month auto policy upfront, collects nine hundred dollars in cash on day one, pays out roughly seven hundred eighty-seven dollars in claims and expenses—reflecting Progressive's stellar 87.4 percent combined ratio in 2025 across $81.66 billion in earned premiums—keeps the underwriting profit, and earns four to five percent bond yields on the cash float in the meantime. Chubb executed the same playbook globally in commercial and high-net-worth lines, posting a record-low 85.7 percent combined ratio and $6.53 billion in pure underwriting profit in 2025.

Finally, Consumer Finance makes up 3.76 percent, headlined by American Express. Unlike Visa's open four-party network, Amex runs a closed loop: it issues the card, runs the network, and signs the merchant. When a consultant pays an annual membership fee for an Amex Platinum card and charges a one-thousand-dollar flight, Amex captures the full 2.24 percent merchant discount fee—more than twenty-two dollars—directly, alongside $136 in annualized card fees per member as of Q3 2026. Put all five engines together, and you see why XLF is no longer a one-trick interest-rate trade: it is a five-cylinder toll-booth on American commerce, credit, capital formation, and risk transfer.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION — Five Cylinders That Offset Each Other Across the Cycle
paragraphs: Notice the internal diversification built into XLF's five segments. When interest rates fall and compress bank net interest margins, lower borrowing costs typically ignite corporate bond issuance and M&A fees at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and S&P Global. When equity markets wobble and slow asset-management inflows, Visa and Mastercard still collect tolls on everyday groceries and travel while Chubb and Progressive collect mandatory auto and commercial insurance premiums. Understanding which cylinder is firing—and which is stalling—is the key to reading XLF's earnings cycle.

book_subsections.heading: How the Next Sixty-Six Holdings Complete the Financial Ecosystem
paragraphs: Because XLF's top ten holdings command 57.17 percent of the fund, it is easy to forget the sixty-six other S&P 500 financial franchises sharing the remaining 42.83 percent. Yet that second tier holds some of the most durable toll-booths in modern finance. Inside Capital Markets, you own the core plumbing of global trading and credit allocation: CME Group and Intercontinental Exchange running futures and clearinghouses, S&P Global and Moody's stamping credit ratings on corporate debt, MSCI licensing global equity benchmarks, and alternative-asset heavyweights like Blackstone, KKR, and Apollo gathering long-dated institutional capital.

Inside Insurance, you own not just Chubb and Progressive, but also global insurance brokers Marsh & McLennan and Aon—capital-light intermediaries that collect commissions on commercial property and reinsurance placements without taking a single dollar of catastrophe risk on their own balance sheets. When insurance premiums rise during hard markets, brokers earn higher dollar fees automatically with zero hurricane or wildfire liability. Alongside them sit Travelers, Allstate, MetLife, and Aflac, diversifying XLF across commercial specialty lines, personal auto, and supplemental life coverage.

And inside Banking and Financial Services, the mid-tier rounds out the U.S. economy's everyday plumbing: super-regional lenders like U.S. Bancorp, PNC Financial, and Truist; merchant-acquiring and core-banking software processors like Fiserv and Fidelity National Information Services; and consumer-credit franchises like Capital One. When you step back and look at all seventy-six holdings together, you realize why XLF behaves like a cross-section of American capitalism's nervous system: every mortgage, corporate bond, payroll check, hotel swipe, freight policy, and retirement ETF passes through at least one constituent inside this ticker.
